name: Zonguldak
title: Zonguldak Thickness Measurement | Coal and Bulk Carrier UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Zonguldak for coal and bulk carriers at the port, the power station jetties and the open anchorage: holds, tanks and decks.
h1: Ship Hull and Hold Gauging at Zonguldak and the Western Black Sea Coal Coast
intro: Zonguldak is Turkey's historic coal port, and the coast around it still moves coal, power-station fuel and bulk cargo through exposed Black Sea berths. Ships that call here are bulk carriers and coasters working abrasive cargoes, often at berths where the swell decides the day. Our technicians travel from India to the vessel, and we fit gauging into the discharge sequence or the anchorage wait, with holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks as the usual scope.

highlights.p: Coal and similar dry bulks are hard on tank tops, lower hold frames and hatch coamings, and wet coal accelerates corrosion. Readings here show owners where the steel really stands before the next docking.
The coast has little natural shelter, so berthing and launch work depend on sea state. We plan with a priority list so the most useful readings are taken in the calm spells.
Zonguldak's own port, the coal-fired power plant jetties at Çatalağzı and the newer terminals along the coast can be linked in a single road-based mobilisation when the ships' windows overlap.

port.h: Zonguldak: coal harbour on an exposed coast
p: Zonguldak lies on the western Black Sea coast of Turkey, east of Ereğli, in a hilly region long known for hard coal mining. The city's port and the jetties along the nearby shore were built to export and receive coal, and the area is still tied to energy: a coal-fired power station at Çatalağzı takes imported coal by sea, steelworks in the region need coking coal and ore, and the state mining company's output has historically gone through these berths. The coast faces the open Black Sea to the north, so northerly swell can make berths and anchorages uncomfortable.

The ship mix is mostly dry bulk. Panamax and Supramax carriers bring coal for the power plant and for industry, smaller Handysize and coaster tonnage works regional cargoes, and general cargo ships carry project and steel material. Many of these ships are middle-aged or older and trade across the Black Sea, the Marmara and the Mediterranean on tight schedules. Coal, especially when wet, causes steady corrosion of tank tops, hold frames and the lower parts of bulkheads, and the grabs used for discharge damage plating, so structural condition is a standing concern for owners and for the surveyors attending the ships.

Gauging demand reflects both condition and timing. Owners want evidence of wastage before they commit to steel renewal, charterers want holds and hatch covers checked, and buyers of second-hand bulkers want readings before closing. A ship waiting for a berth may lie at anchor for days when the weather is poor, which creates time for ballast tanks and deck work, but also unpredictable interruptions. The area has no large commercial drydock for ocean-going ships, so Zonguldak is usually a place to collect the preliminary scope rather than to complete a renewal survey.

At the discharge berths, holds are gauged as they are emptied and swept. The gang cleaning the tank top and the grab driver both need the hold, so the superintendent and the master agree the sequence and we step in when a hold is released with the entry permit issued. Hatch covers and coamings can be measured at the same time from the deck. Because the berths are exposed, a swell that stops cargo work can also stop access by gangway, and the plan allows for lost hours.

Ships at anchor off Zonguldak are reached by launch arranged through the agent. The sea state here can change within hours, so we take the highest-priority items first: ballast tank plating in the topside and hopper tanks, deck plating around the hatch corners and the readings that decide a docking date. For ships moving on to a yard, we provide an organised set of readings by frame and strake that the yard can use for its steel estimate, rather than a raw list that has to be sorted on arrival.
list: Zonguldak port coal berths — hold, tank-top and hatch cover gauging on bulk carriers as holds are released during discharge
Çatalağzı power-station jetties — gauging on coal carriers during their call, subject to the terminal's safety and ISPS rules
Terminals along the nearby coast — bulk and general cargo ships gauged during loading and discharge on one road-based mobilisation
Open anchorage off the coast — deck and ballast tank readings on ships waiting for a berth, by launch when the sea allows
Pre-docking steel scope — frames, bulkheads and plating organised by strake for a yard in the Marmara or elsewhere

context.h: Port state control and the energy trades of the Black Sea coast
p: Turkish ports are covered by both the Black Sea MoU and the Mediterranean MoU on port state control, and the Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure and the local harbour masters administer ship safety and port operations. Bulk carriers trading in coal and steel are a regular focus of inspection because hatch covers, coamings and hold structure deteriorate quickly in these trades. A deficiency recorded at a Black Sea port often prompts an owner to extend the gauging scope to adjacent plating before the ship is next inspected.

The Black Sea lies outside the emission control areas, so ships here follow the global fuel limit, though a ship sailing on to the Marmara enters the Mediterranean ECA. Coal imports for power generation are shaped by energy policy, and tonnage employed on these runs ranges widely in age. Ships that will later call at European Union ports need a valid Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and those voyages fall under EU ETS. For managers, the practical result is that steel records taken at a coal call help justify docking decisions and charter negotiations later.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Zonguldak
jobs.p: Typical jobs here are driven by coal and bulk calls. A Panamax discharging at a power-station jetty gives hold access in sequence, a coaster at the port gives a short stay with a few holds, and a ship waiting at anchor gives time for ballast tanks and deck. Superintendents usually want a documented steel scope for the next docking, and charterers sometimes ask for hold and hatch condition evidence.
list: Tank-top and lower hold frame gauging on a Panamax bulk carrier discharging coal at a power-station jetty, before a docking planned in the Marmara.
Hatch cover, coaming and deck gauging on a coaster at the Zonguldak port berths, with readings handed to the technical department before the ship sails.
Ballast tank gauging on a Supramax waiting at the anchorage for a berth, concentrated on topside and hopper tanks that the crew have ventilated.
Condition gauging for a time-charter delivery on a Handysize bulker, recording holds and hatches for owner and charterer.
Magnetic particle inspection of hatch-corner and bracket welds on an older bulker after grab damage and cracking were noted during discharge.

logistics: The team flies into Istanbul and continues by road to Zonguldak, a longer overland journey than for ports near the Marmara. Zonguldak also has a small regional airport whose services come and go, so we do not rely on it. Berth passes under ISPS, power-station jetty permits and anchorage launches are arranged through the ship's agent, with crew lists and certificates sent ahead. Indian passport holders need a Turkish visa, which we apply for once a call is probable and renew if the ship's schedule moves.

faqs.q: Can a coal carrier be gauged at a power-station jetty?
faqs.a: Usually yes, in the holds once they are released. The jetty operator sets safety and access rules, and the master controls enclosed-space entry. We gauge tank tops, lower frames and bulkheads as holds are swept, and take hatch covers and coamings from the deck. The plan follows the discharge sequence and is agreed with the superintendent beforehand.

faqs.q: Is it realistic to complete a special survey gauging programme at Zonguldak?
faqs.a: Rarely. There is no large drydock for ocean-going ships here, and a full programme includes shell and bottom plating that is reached in dock. What Zonguldak does well is give early readings of holds, hatches and ballast tanks, so the owner and yard have a measured steel estimate before the ship arrives for the survey.

faqs.q: How does rough weather affect work at the anchorage?
faqs.a: It can stop launches altogether, and a northerly swell makes boarding unsafe. We therefore avoid promising a fixed day, keep a priority list and move to interior work, such as tanks, when deck access is not possible. If the weather turns and the ship has to berth or sail, the readings already taken are reported as they stand.

faqs.q: Can you gauge hatch covers on a ship loading or discharging coal?
faqs.a: Hatch covers that are closed and clear of working gear can be gauged from the deck, and open panels can be measured when the cranes or grabs are away. Safety around cargo gear comes first, so work in way of the hatches is coordinated with the mate. Coamings and cross-deck plating are usually accessible throughout the stay.
